Andrew Johnson's inauguration. On April 15, 1865, Andrew Johnson assumed the presidency under the most traumatic circumstances imaginable. Lincoln had been assassinated just the evening before. Johnson had not attended Lincoln's second inauguration weeks earlier. Instead, he was notified of the presidency by telegram while traveling. Johnson was a Tennessee tailor with little formal education and deep regional prejudices that would shape his approach to the country's greatest crisis. Unlike his predecessors, he gave no formal inaugural address, instead issuing brief, hastily drafted remarks. His Reconstruction policies would prove far harsher on freedmen and more lenient toward the South than Lincoln's vision implied. Johnson's approach favored rapid Southern readmission to the Union with minimal protections for freedmen. He openly held racist views and opposed voting rights for Black Americans. Opposed to the Fourteenth Amendment, he vetoed civil rights legislation, setting himself in direct conflict with Republican members of Congress. This ideological split over Reconstruction would eventually lead to his impeachment in 1868 on charges stemming from his conflict with Congressional Republicans, shaping decades of subsequent conflict and suffering.
